sections.h: The night of the TNT area chase
p: Point Pleasant is a small town where the Kanawha River runs into the Ohio. A few miles north of it is the TNT area, which is basically a big patch of woods and ponds with a bunch of concrete igloos left over from a Second World War explosives plant. By 1966 it was where local couples went to park (you know the kind of spot I mean).

Late on November 15, 1966, Roger and Linda Scarberry and Steve and Mary Mallette were driving past the old power plant out there when they saw something standing by the building. They said it was shaped like a man, six or seven feet tall, grey, with wings folded behind it and two big red eyes that lit up in the headlights. They floored it back toward town and both couples swore the thing took off and stayed right above the car, even when they hit 100 miles an hour.

They went straight to the Mason County sheriff's office. A deputy drove back out with them and didn't find anything, but the story was in the Point Pleasant Register the next day and in papers all over the country within a week.

Funny enough, the chase wasn't actually the first report. A few days before, some gravediggers near Clendenin (about 60 miles away) said a brown, man-like figure lifted out of the trees and flew right over them. Then on November 16 Marcella Bennett said a tall grey shape with red eyes rose up beside her car near the TNT area while she was holding her baby daughter. I can't imagine.

Over the next 13 months dozens more people came forward, mostly around the TNT area and the river roads. John Keel, the writer who spent a lot of 1967 down there talking to witnesses, later said it was over 100 people.

What gets me is how much the stories line up. People kept saying there was no real face, just those eyes. The wings never flapped. And it didn't matter how hard the driver floored it, the thing kept up with the car. That's a weird set of details for a bunch of strangers to agree on.

As for the name, a newspaper copy editor usually gets the credit. Batman was a big hit on TV that year so "Mothman" stuck pretty much right away, even though nobody who saw it ever said it looked like a moth.

The first explanation showed up almost right away. Dr. Robert L. Smith, a wildlife biologist at West Virginia University, told reporters he thought the witnesses saw a sandhill crane. Those birds are about four feet tall with a wingspan close to seven feet, and they have a patch of red skin on the forehead right above the eyes that can flash in a car's lights. They weren't common in West Virginia but they do wander off their migration routes now and then.

Other people have pointed at big owls, like a barred owl or a barn owl. Their eyes shine like crazy in headlights and up close in the dark they can look a heck of a lot bigger than they are. And once the story was in the paper, let's face it, every odd shape out in the TNT area was going to get called Mothman.

The witnesses didn't buy the bird idea at all. They said it was the size of a man, stood upright and didn't have a beak or a neck. Honestly I think a crane explains some of the reports and not others, and that's about as far as I can take it.

sections.h: The Silver Bridge and the prophecy legend
p: At rush hour on December 15, 1967 the Silver Bridge between Point Pleasant and Gallipolis, Ohio fell into the river and 46 people died. The investigation found a crack in a single eyebar link in the suspension chain, and the disaster is the reason the US started national bridge inspections.

The sightings mostly stopped after that, and some people started to see Mothman as a warning. Keel ran with that in his 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies, where he mixed the sightings in with UFO reports, weird phone calls and his own run-ins with men in black. The 2002 movie with Richard Gere took the omen version around the world. Side note: the bridge failed because of a cracked eyebar, so I'd give the engineering report more weight than the prophecy.

Point Pleasant went all in on its monster and good for them. The [Mothman Museum](/places/mothman-museum/) has props from the movie and the original newspaper coverage, Bob Roach's shiny steel [Mothman statue](/places/mothman-statue/) stands downtown, and the [Mothman Festival](/places/mothman-festival/) takes over the streets every September. You can even go out to the TNT area, which is a public wildlife management area now, on one of the [guided tours](/places/mothman-tnt-tours/).

The reports haven't really stopped either. In 2017 a run of winged-figure sightings around Chicago got labelled "the Chicago Mothman", and red-eyed flying things still show up in reports from all over North America. The famous cases and the places you can visit are all on the [Mothman map](/map/?creature=mothman).

faq.a: Here's the thing. In all the years since, nobody has come up with a photo that holds up, a body or anything else you could actually hold in your hand. The 1966 and 1967 witnesses were sincere and a lot of them never changed their stories, but most researchers think they saw a big bird in the dark, probably a sandhill crane or an owl. The witnesses themselves said it was man-sized and stood upright, so make of that what you will.

The famous first sighting was at the TNT area, an old explosives plant a few miles north of Point Pleasant, West Virginia, on November 15, 1966. Some gravediggers near Clendenin, West Virginia reported something similar a few days before that.
A newspaper copy editor usually gets the credit, playing off the Batman TV show that was huge in 1966. Nobody who saw it actually said it looked like a moth.

faq.q: Did Mothman cause the Silver Bridge collapse?
faq.a: No. The bridge came down because of a crack in one eyebar link in its suspension chain. The idea that Mothman was a warning comes from John Keel's 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies.

faq.q: What is the difference between Mothman and Owlman?
faq.a: Mothman was West Virginia in 1966 and 1967, grey, sort of headless-looking with red eyes. Owlman was seen near Mawnan church in Cornwall, England starting in 1976 and looked more like a feathered man with an owl's face. We put them side by side in [Mothman vs Owlman](/compare/mothman-vs-owlman/).

Indrid Cold is the smiling man in a dark suit that Woodrow Derenberger said stepped out of a landed craft near Parkersburg, West Virginia on November 2, 1966, two weeks before the TNT area chase. John Keel linked the two stories. Here's more on [Indrid Cold](/creatures/indrid-cold/).
Every September in downtown Point Pleasant, usually the third weekend. Our [Mothman Festival](/places/mothman-festival/) page has this year's dates.
